clue.text: Matches at Chelsea entertaining one carrying books?

indicators.note: to entertain is to host or hold, so the phrase before it holds the run of letters inside it

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and into the next two

explanation.surface: Football fixtures at Stamford Bridge play host to a fan lugging books.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea is a London football club, which makes 'Matches' read as games rather than as letters to search.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolbag with a shoulder strap is what pupils use for carrying their textbooks, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Prophet tucked into South American snack

indicators.note: something tucked into another thing sits inside it, so the prophet goes inside

explanation.surface: A holy man eats his food while in South America.
explanation.walkthrough: Amos is a minor prophet of the Old Testament, one of the twelve whose books close it.
explanation.definitionFit: A samosa is a fried triangular pastry with spiced filling, eaten as a small savoury bite between meals.

clue.text: Head of troubled university going to sort out staff

indicators.note: to sort something out is to rearrange it, so these letters are put into a new order
the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

explanation.surface: A troubled university's leader is off to reorganise the employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort out staff' reads as a management task, but 'sort' is the fodder and 'out' its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutors make up the teaching personnel of a college, so they are its academic employees collectively.

clue.text: Hitler and Luftwaffe finally prepared to keep officer in aircraft

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the officer is held within the other letters
prepared means made ready or worked up, so the letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: the name rearranged; as printed it is one letter short

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Nazi leader and his air force get ready to carry an officer aboard a plane.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed the fodder is one letter short: Hitler supplies no P, and no other word does, so the setter has slipped.
explanation.definitionFit: A helicopter is a rotor-driven flying machine, one kind of aircraft.

clue.text: Colour of worthless item

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a pale yellow shade
second meaning: a dud, especially a faulty car or product

explanation.walkthrough: 'of' joins the two meanings, making them look like one phrase about the colour of a cheap object.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a pale yellow hue, and colloquially a defective purchase that proves useless.

clue.text: Symbol in text is ring over loop

parts.note: the sound a bell makes when it rings

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the word for loop is read the other way round

parts.note: a tab is a small loop or flap of fabric for hanging something

explanation.surface: A typographer explains that a certain character in a document is a circle above a curl.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'over' as one shape placed on another, but it is the turnaround signal for the loop word.
explanation.definitionFit: A dingbat is a typographical ornament or pictorial character, like those in the Zapf Dingbats font, set among printed words.

clue.text: West Indian academic taking car to California

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it, so the car goes inside the academic

parts.note: a don is a university lecturer

explanation.surface: A Caribbean lecturer drives his vehicle over to the American West Coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' here simply means 'next to', placing CA after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Dominica or the Dominican Republic comes from the Caribbean islands collectively called the West Indies.

clue.text: Beginner returning favour …

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a boon is a favour or blessing

explanation.surface: A newcomer pays back a kindness, with the ellipsis carrying the thought into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Noob is internet slang for a newbie, a novice who has only just started at a game or activity.

clue.text: … Supports housing a minister in military accommodation

indicators.note: housing something means giving it a home inside, so these letters sit within the supports

parts.note: to back someone is to support them
Right Reverend, the title of a senior clergyman

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, backers shelter a government minister inside army quarters.
explanation.walkthrough: A minister here is a clergyman, not a politician, so the abbreviation is the Right Reverend's title; the ellipsis links it to the clue before.
explanation.definitionFit: Barracks are the buildings where soldiers live, a lodging block for troops.

clue.text: Note on mobile model about start of regeneration for tardis user

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so the letters move into a new order
in a down clue one piece on another sits above it, so the note comes first

parts.note: the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters wrap round one letter
the start of a word is its opening letter only

explanation.surface: A memo stuck on a phone about the start of a regeneration, addressed to the TARDIS owner.
explanation.walkthrough: In Doctor Who, the TARDIS is the time machine and the Doctor regenerates into a new body; 'mobile' looks like a phone but signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Doctor is a Time Lord, the alien race that pilots the police-box TARDIS through space and history.

clue.text: Dummy swapping diamonds for time in temporary accommodation

indicators.note: swapping X for Y means removing one letter and putting another in its place

parts.note: a tailor's dummy is a model

explanation.surface: A mannequin trades jewels for some time in a short-stay lodging.
explanation.walkthrough: The D in MODEL is replaced by T.
explanation.definitionFit: A motel is a roadside hotel for motorists, where guests stay only a night or two.

clue.text: Medical examination for relative with second pulse

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
gram is a pulse, a type of legume such as chickpea

explanation.surface: A family member with a second heartbeat reading needs a medical check-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulse' tempts as a heartbeat, but here it is the edible seed of a legume.
explanation.definitionFit: A mammogram is an X-ray of the breast used to screen for cancer, a clinical test.

clue.text: Second attempt to get hydrogen and nitrogen into surprisingly nice poison

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside, so these two letters go within
a surprising version is unexpected, so the letters turn up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A chemist's second try at mixing elements into something pleasant produces a toxin.
explanation.walkthrough: H and N go together between the C and the INE of the rearranged nice.
explanation.definitionFit: Strychnine is a highly toxic plant alkaloid long used as rat killer and in murder mysteries.

clue.text: Dog in river leaving scent

indicators.note: the river abbreviation is leaving, so it is taken out of the word that follows

parts.note: a scent trail left behind for hounds to follow

explanation.surface: A hound wades into a stream and loses the smell it was tracking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog' is a verb here, meaning to follow closely, not the animal in the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail someone is to follow them secretly, just as to dog their steps is to shadow them.

clue.text: Sage mixes a cocktail for second Sunday in Lent

definitions.note: strictly it is the second Sunday before Lent

indicators.note: mixing a cocktail stirs ingredients together, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; the verb doubles as fodder

explanation.surface: A wise man shakes up a drink to mark a Sunday in the church calendar.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is 'Sage mixes a', with 'mixes' doing double duty as letters and as part of the signal; the clue slightly misplaces the Sunday, which falls before Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: Sexagesima is the Sunday about sixty days before Easter, in the pre-Lent sequence of the church year.

clue.text: Potter's electronic tool?

parts.note: surface reading: a ceramicist's powered gadget, like an electric wheel
setter's reading: Harry Potter, the boy wizard, who would need something to verify his magic incantations

explanation.walkthrough: A potter suggests clay and kilns, but the capital hides Harry Potter, and a wizard's magic words are spells.
explanation.definitionFit: Word-processing software flags misspelt words; punningly, a wizard's device would vet his incantations.

clue.text: Liberal listened to criminal and thief

indicators.note: something listened to is heard rather than seen, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a fire-raiser, one kind of criminal, said out loud

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician heard out a crook and a robber.
explanation.walkthrough: L-arsonist said out loud gives the sound of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Larceny is the legal term for theft, so a person who commits it is a stealer of goods.

clue.text: Fools mostly stood up for judge

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means read from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards
mostly means all but a little, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to rise is to stand up

explanation.surface: Idiots mostly rose on behalf of the magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: ROSE loses its E and is then turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor evaluates and gives a verdict on something, as a judge appraises a case or a competition.

clue.text: Good decoration on stamp books

parts.note: Order of the British Empire, an honour
a die is a tool that stamps a design
New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A medal pictured on a postage stamp next to some volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: OBE is a British honour, the Order of the British Empire; 'on' just places the pieces one after another.
explanation.definitionFit: Good as said to a child or a dog means well-behaved, doing what it is told.

clue.text: Urban set near newly built underground

indicators.note: something newly built is put together afresh, so the letters are assembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A city development near a freshly constructed metro line.
explanation.definitionFit: Subterranean describes anything beneath the earth's surface, exactly as below-ground does.

clue.text: Central ingredient in bread featuring in food waste lists

indicators.note: featuring in means appearing inside, so the letter goes within the other word
the central ingredient of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A recipe note: the main element of a loaf appears among leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lists' is a verb, as a ship lists; it is not the noun for written items.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship that lists leans to one side, and a surface that slopes is likewise tilted.

clue.text: Confused clergyman taken in by dodgy deal

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable, so the letters are not to be trusted in their order
taken in by means held inside, so the clergyman sits within

explanation.surface: A muddled vicar is conned by a shady bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: Addled means muddled or unable to think clearly, as a befuddled mind is.

clue.text: Whirlwind decapitated cuddly toy

indicators.note: decapitating removes the head, so the opening letter goes

explanation.surface: A storm rips the head off a child's soft toy.
explanation.definitionFit: An eddy is a swirling circular current of air or water, a small whirl.

clue.text: Spring cured so-called rich

parts.note: a spring is a water source

indicators.note: so-called means named or called out, pointing to how the word is heard

explanation.surface: Taking the waters at a spa supposedly cures the wealthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-heeled is an idiom for affluent, from having good shoes rather than worn ones.

clue.text: Furious athlete losing three extremities in revolving machine

indicators.note: furious suggests wild agitation, so the remaining letters are thrown about
losing means giving up, so those letters are removed
a word's extremities are its two end letters

explanation.surface: An angry sportsman loses three limbs in a spinning machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three extremities' looks like a count of limbs, but it means the ends of the word three; one T and one E leave athlete before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A lathe is a workshop tool that spins a workpiece so it can be shaped by a cutter.

clue.text: Poacher nearly catching bird

indicators.note: catching means holding, so the run of letters is held within the words before

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A poacher almost bags a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' looks like it trims a word, but it is just part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, a crossword favourite among birds.

clue.text: Flavouring made from small fruit in perfect condition

explanation.surface: A food label says this taste comes from small, flawless fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Spearmint is a herb whose oil is used to give taste to chewing gum and toothpaste.

clue.text: Force independent politician to meet the Spanish

explanation.surface: Pressuring an unaffiliated MP into a meeting with Spanish counterparts.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to drive or compel someone to act, just as to force them is.

clue.text: Queen stopping King Edward, say, being sent back to refuge

indicators.note: sent back means returned the way it came, so the whole is read backwards
stopping something plugs a gap in it, so the queen sits inside

parts.note: King Edward is a British potato variety; tater is slang for potato

explanation.surface: A queen blocks a king and he is exiled to a sanctuary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King Edward, say' suggests a monarch, but it is a variety of potato, so 'say' marks an example; ER goes after TA.
explanation.definitionFit: A retreat is a quiet place to withdraw to, a sanctuary or haven.

clue.text: Priest in newly sealed container slipped away

indicators.note: newly means made afresh, so the letters are rearranged
placed in means sitting inside, so the priest goes within
names the rearranged word as the holder, which wraps round the priest

explanation.surface: A cleric shut inside a sealed box has passed away.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that has elapsed has passed by, gone without being noticed, the way something slips off.
